text: In 1959, nine hikers in the Soviet Ural Mountains cut their way out of their own tent...
and walked into the freezing dark.
They were experienced. Most were students from the Ural Polytechnic Institute.
Their leader was twenty-three-year-old Igor Dyatlov.
On the night of February first, they camped on a bare, open slope.
The local Mansi people called the mountain Kholat Syakhl. Dead Mountain.
They never came back.
Weeks later, searchers found the tent, half buried in snow.
It had been cut open... from the inside.
Their boots were still inside.
Footprints in socks and bare feet led down the slope, toward the forest.
The first of them were found by a cedar tree, beside the remains of a small fire.
The last four weren't found until May, deep in a ravine.
Some had injuries investigators struggled to explain.
Some of their clothing reportedly showed traces of radiation.
The Soviet investigation blamed a compelling natural force, and closed the case.
In 2020, Russian prosecutors concluded it was an avalanche.
But many people still don't believe it.
Why would nine experienced hikers run into the night without their boots?
What do you think happened on Dead Mountain?
